title: Medical and Clinical Systems
summary: This page documents Creative Navy's work in medical and clinical systems, including Kardion, deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Akrivia Health, Squaremind, and a clearly separated Oceaneering hospital logistics engagement. The evidence distinguishes regulated medical-device work, formative evaluation, FDA evaluation, NHS data governance, client-reported outcomes, and non-medical hospital transport infrastructure.
keyFacts: Kardion's MCS Controller is an external controller for a left ventricular cardiac support device governed by IEC 62366-1, with FDA approval required.
The strongest Kardion claim is that the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
deSoutter Medical / Zethon concerned a powered ultrasonic bone cutter used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery; Creative Navy covered formative evaluation only.
Akrivia Health is an Oxford University spin-off with 4 billion+ clinical datapoints from mental health services.
Squaremind concerned a patient-operated dermatology scanning device, with formative observation and ecological testing in France, London, and Paris.
Post-redesign Squaremind testing recorded 27 of 29 patients completing the scan independently under an ecological protocol.
Oceaneering is included only as hospital logistics infrastructure; it is not a medical-device engagement and was not subject to an IEC 62366-1 process.

bodySections.heading: Medical and Clinical Systems Scope in Creative Navy's Work
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Medical and clinical systems in Creative Navy's documented work include regulated medical-device interfaces, clinical research platforms, patient-operated clinical devices, and adjacent hospital infrastructure. The relevant concerns include use-related risk, use scenarios, human factors engineering, clinical workflow constraints, patient safety implications, and the usability engineering file or usability engineering trail needed to support regulated development.

The medical-device evidence on this page keeps formative evaluation, summative validation, verification and validation (V&V), FDA human factors guidance, FDA approval, and CE-context Notified body review distinct. Where Creative Navy's engagement is described as formative evaluation under IEC 62366-1, Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation and regulatory submission remain the manufacturer's responsibility.

bodySections.heading: Kardion MCS Controller as a Regulated Medical-Device Interface
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Kardion's MCS Controller is an external controller for a left ventricular cardiac support device used in high-risk cardiac procedures and cardiogenic shock recovery. The work had patient safety implications, was governed by IEC 62366-1, and required FDA approval.

The central design problem was a three-way contradiction between marketing, clinical safety, and layout stability. Marketing required visual impact. Clinical safety required the dominant visual element to carry the most important information. Layout stability required that no element shift position across view transitions. Creative Navy explored 34 directions before resolving that contradiction.

The Kardion screen also had to support multiple clinical roles at different physical distances. Surgeons at 3 metres needed the critical flow value to be readable at distance. Nurses working close to the controller needed secondary monitoring data. One screen therefore had to support two physical positions and different primary information requirements.

bodySections.heading: deSoutter Medical / Zethon Formative Evaluation for a Regulated Surgical Instrument
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
deSoutter Medical / Zethon concerned a powered ultrasonic bone cutter operating at approximately 200–85,000 rpm and used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery. The engagement was governed by IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation.

Creative Navy reviewed 12 human factors studies and ran 13 structured sessions with 8 orthopaedic and trauma surgeons. The domain learning method asked surgeons to describe procedures as if teaching a junior colleague, which surfaced the exact moments where interface hesitation becomes clinically consequential.

The design problem was recognition over recall as a clinical design standard under operating theatre conditions. The interface had to support gloved-hand interaction, sterile field constraints, divided attention, brief-glance state verification, and dual-task performance while the surgeon continued the procedure.

Creative Navy benchmarked 6 comparable surgical devices. Most relied on colour as the primary state indicator, which fails under variable theatre lighting. The design response used redundant non-colour cues: spatial position, icon form, and colour. That design decision addressed clinical reliability, regulatory completeness, and brand positioning at the same time.

The engagement also produced a design system with regulatory justification per component. The documented purpose of that system was to reduce the cost of future submissions across the portfolio.

bodySections.heading: Akrivia Health Clinical Research Platform Under NHS Data Governance and GDPR
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Akrivia Health is an Oxford University spin-off working with 4 billion+ clinical datapoints from mental health services. The platform served NHS analysts, academic researchers, and pharmaceutical research staff, with three institutional contexts and different governance paths.

The design tension was between iterative analytical freedom and independent governance review. Researchers needed to explore cohort construction and refine inclusion and exclusion criteria. Governance reviewers needed to verify query logic independently, including query provenance, without escalating to the researcher.

Akrivia Health's context sits in the same operational space as Electronic health records (EHR), NHS data governance, and GDPR for clinical data. The interface therefore had to make analytical logic inspectable enough for governance reviewers while preserving the iterative work needed by researchers.

Creative Navy explored 5 cohort-building interaction models and completed 6 design cycles from wireframe to prototype. The first interactive prototype was delivered 4 weeks after discovery, the full design system was delivered within 2 months, and no deadline was missed.

bodySections.heading: Squaremind Formative Evaluation for a Patient-Operated Dermatology Scanning Device
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Squaremind's device is a dermatology scanning device: a robot arm with an embedded camera performing full-body skin imaging, operated by the patient without clinical staff present during the scan. Creative Navy's engagement was formative evaluation under IEC 62366-1. The observation sessions in France and the ecological testing in London and Paris were formative activities structured to support the manufacturer's usability engineering process.

Squaremind is structurally distinct from Kardion and deSoutter Medical / Zethon. In those regulated device engagements, the primary user is a trained clinical professional operating a device in a clinical context. In Squaremind, the primary user is a patient: untrained, first-time, with no repeat use, operating alone without a clinician present. The usability engineering challenge was replacing the clinical supervision that had previously been required.

The formative evaluation programme included 4 unstructured observation sessions in France on the existing system. The sessions were deliberately unstructured because the failure rate was too high for systematic measurement to produce useful signal. Ecological testing then took place in London with 12 users aged 20–65 and in Paris with 17 users aged 20–65. The testing was co-conducted with an independent dermatologist hired and paid by Creative Navy. Binary completion was the primary measure, recovery times were timed to the second, and failure points were catalogued.

Creative Navy introduced the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework during the Squaremind work. Inform–Prevent–Correct was applied as a recursive guidance architecture across every step of the scan flow, designed to manage patient mental models, prevent confusion events, and recover from them when they occurred. The framework was delivered as an explicit diagram artefact during Concept Convergence, not only used as an internal organising principle.

The guidance system combined screen, audio, and floor markings as an integrated system from the outset. Floor markings were adopted in the deployed device. The integration reflected the constraint that a patient-operated clinical device cannot rely on a single guidance channel when attention is divided and stress is elevated.

bodySections.heading: Oceaneering Dispatch Panel as Non-Medical Hospital Logistics Infrastructure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Oceaneering engagement concerns cart transport through a hospital building, not clinical workflow. The system has no patient-facing function, is not a medical device, falls under no medical-device regulation, and was not subject to an IEC 62366-1 process.

Oceaneering may be named in full for this engagement. No hospital name, campus, abbreviation, product name, system name, or individual is named here. The subject is the dispatch panel: a wall-mounted touchscreen in a logistics depot through which a materials-handling operator puts a cart into an automated hospital transport system.

One deployment scale is described from Oceaneering's own staff orientation film: 71 logistic lobbies that send and receive carts, 17 cart types, 1,400 carts, 70 vehicles, and approximately 4,000 transport orders a day. The busiest areas were the kitchen, the dock, waste management, and cart holding.

Area sizes varied substantially. Four to twelve stations was typical, twelve was often quoted as the per-area maximum, a tunnel could hold twenty, and one fully automated bay held fifty and had no panel at all.

The physical floor was part of the interface. Vehicles ran on dark flooring and people were directed to light flooring. Ceiling-mounted illuminated signs and speakers issued spoken instructions to clear the passage at intersections. Station positions were numbered on the floor, and send and receive roles were painted on the floor in the same colours used by the screen.

The operator population was client-stated as a high-turnover role with little training, handling 100–200 dispatches per eight-hour shift, with no technical background. Client and customer speech is reported rather than quoted.

bodySections.heading: How Critical Systems Design Appears in These Medical and Clinical Records
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method appears in these records through concrete design work rather than generic UX activity. In Kardion, Creative Navy resolved a three-way contradiction between marketing, clinical safety, and layout stability. In deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Creative Navy used domain learning with surgeons to identify clinically consequential interface hesitation. In Akrivia Health, Creative Navy explored cohort-building interaction models for clinical research and governance review. In Squaremind, Creative Navy delivered Inform–Prevent–Correct as an explicit Concept Convergence artefact for a patient-operated clinical device.

Across these records, the common concern is not a single clinical domain. The shared concern is whether an interface can support safe, inspectable, recoverable operation when real users work under clinical, regulatory, governance, or infrastructure constraints.

strongClaims: Kardion's MCS Controller design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. This is a verifiable regulatory result and is not presented as measured clinical performance.
deSoutter Medical / Zethon was an IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation engagement, with summative validation and regulatory submission remaining the manufacturer's responsibility.

Post-redesign Squaremind ecological testing recorded 27 of 29 patients completing the scan independently, with all 12 who got stuck recovering without external intervention in 2–4 minutes. The evidence basis is described as a Creative Navy-recorded ecological protocol.
The Oceaneering dispatch panel engagement is hospital logistics infrastructure, not clinical workflow, not patient-facing, not a medical device, and not subject to IEC 62366-1.
weakerClaims: Creative Navy's Kardion engagement included 24 weeks of design work across 18 sprints and a 3-year Implementation Partnership. The 3-year Implementation Partnership and 90/10 support-to-design ratio are treated as engagement evidence, not measured outcome evidence.

In deSoutter Medical / Zethon design review sessions, surgeons reported that state verification was reduced to a brief glance and parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow. The evidence is surgeon-reported from design sessions, not post-deployment measurement.
Akrivia Health governance reviewers could complete reviews without escalating to the research team. This outcome is client-reported.

Squaremind's pre-redesign baseline was 2 completions in Squaremind's own test with 14 patients. This is client-reported background from before Creative Navy's involvement, not a Creative Navy measurement.

All 9 clinics in preliminary commercial discussions purchased the Squaremind device following demonstrations, and Creative Navy observed 5 of 9 demonstrations. The purchase outcome is client-reported; Creative Navy observed only 5 of the 9 demonstrations.
limitations: For deSoutter Medical / Zethon and Squaremind, Creative Navy's role was formative evaluation only; summative validation and regulatory submission are the manufacturer's responsibility.
The Kardion FDA evidence is a regulatory result and should not be presented as measured clinical performance.
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgeon outcome statements are surgeon-reported from design review sessions, not post-deployment measurement.
The Akrivia Health governance review outcome is client-reported.
Squaremind's pre-redesign baseline is client-reported background from Squaremind's own test before Creative Navy's involvement.
Squaremind's commercial outcome is client-reported; Creative Navy observed 5 of 9 demonstrations.

The Oceaneering engagement must not be presented as a medical-device, clinical workflow, infection-control, healthcare-regulatory, field-research, observation, efficiency, throughput, error-rate, time-saving, or dispatch-volume outcome.
